newsitem.title: USA: Sewage, trash can fuel world food output.
newsitem.headline: Sewage, trash can fuel world food output.

text.p: Trash and sewage -- two municipal headaches around the world -- could become a valuable source of water and fertiliser for farmers, researchers said on Monday at a World Bank conference.

The result would be more food and fewer worries about overflowing landfills, they said. It could also mean less disease if farmers had "cleaner" water supplies instead of the polluted water now used for irrigation in parts of the world.
"We have seen them (waste products) as a problem, not a solution," said Anders Wijkman of the U.N. Development Programme in asking that recycling be part of government planning.

Only a small part of the organic waste generated in cities now is turned into compost or other products that would boost farm productivity. The World Bank estimated more than five million people die each year from diseases caused by improper garbage and sewage disposal.

Along with describing beneficial uses, researchers warned that care must be taken to insure there were no plant or human health risks from recycling munincipal wastes. Wijkman, for example, said householders would have to sort their trash to keep harmful items out of organic waste headed for compost.

A $520 million sewage treatment project in Santiago, Chile, was cited as an example of how to turn a pollution problem into a benefit for city dwellers and farmers. Other case studies looked at using Los Angeles sludge as a crop fertiliser and using "renovated" sewage water for industrial plants in Madras, India.

For years, farmers downstream from Santiago often had no choice during the dry summer months than to use river water tainted with city sewage to irrigate fruits, vegetables and other crops. The crops then became a link in the spread of typhoid.

"The spillovers from pollution in the city of Santiago have come back to haunt the city," said Carl Bartone, a World Bank enviromental specialist, who outlined plans to build three wastewater treatment plants for Santiago.
In Madras, industrial use of purified wastewater eased the demands for water in a city short on water supplies.

Kenny Evans, who uses sewage sludge as fertiliser on an Arizona farm covering 22 square miles (5,698 hectares), was among three speakers who said high standards must be set to prevent use of material containing harmful metals, plant-killing organisms or microbes that would sicken people.
